pack.overview: This unit introduces the Turing machine (TM), Alan Turing's simple, intuitive, and generic model that formalizes computation as performed by a human mind. It covers the formal 6-tuple definition, how TMs execute via configurations and transitions, worked constructions (erasing, copying, recognizing regular and non-context-free languages), comparisons with DFAs and PDAs, and the notion of a Universal Turing Machine. Understanding TMs matters because they are the most powerful standard model of computation and underpin the theory of what can and cannot be computed.
learning_objectives: The student will be able to explain Turing's aim and the human-computation analogy (paper=tape, pencil=head, thinking=transition/states).
The student will be able to state the formal 6-tuple definition of a Turing machine and describe the role of each component.
The student will be able to interpret and trace a transition function using a transition table or state diagram, producing the sequence of configurations for a given input.
The student will be able to construct or read TMs that perform computational tasks such as erasing and copying strings and recognizing languages like {a^n b^n c^n | n≥1}.
The student will be able to compare the computational power of DFAs, PDAs, and TMs across memory, halting, and language classes.
The student will be able to define a computation, configuration, and the yields relation for a TM.
The student will be able to define a Universal Turing Machine and explain why universal DFAs/CFGs do not exist while a universal TM does.

key_definitions.definition: A 6-tuple M = (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q0, H) consisting of a finite set of states, input alphabet, tape alphabet, transition function, start state, and set of halting states, formalizing computation with a tape, read/write head, and finite control.
A finite set of states, simulating the states of a human mind during computation.
A finite set of input/output symbols; Σ excludes the left-end symbol ▷, the blank □, and the movement symbols ← and →.
A finite set of symbols that may appear on the tape, with Σ ∪ {▷, □} ⊆ Γ; Γ excludes ← and →.

A function δ: (Q−H)×Γ → Q×(Γ∪{←,→}) that, for a non-halting state and current tape symbol, gives a new state and either a symbol to write or a movement, such that the head never falls off the left end or erases ▷.
The initial state, an element of Q, in which the TM begins its computation.
The set of halting states H = {q_acc, q_rej}, a subset of Q, for which δ is not defined; the machine stops upon reaching them.
The symbol marking the left end of the tape; when the head reads ▷ it must move right so the machine never falls off the left end.
The blank symbol filling tape cells that contain no input or written data.
The TM component that simulates unlimited sheets of paper; it holds the input initially and the output finally.
The read/write head that reads and writes a single tape cell and moves left or right.
The complete information about a computation at one moment: the current state, the tape-head position, and the tape content, e.g., (q4, ▷bbb□).
A sequence of successive configurations C0 ⊢M C1 ⊢M ... ; the yields relation ⊢M steps between configurations and ⊢*M denotes any number of steps.
A TM MU that can simulate the execution of any TM M on any input w, halting iff M halts on w and returning M's result (accept/reject or computed function value).

segments.title: Turing's aim: formalizing human computation
segments.content:
Alan Turing set out to design a model of computation with four qualities: it should be **simple**, **intuitive**, **generic**, and it should **formalize the computation performed by a human mind**. Rather than inventing something exotic, Turing looked at how an ordinary person actually computes.

Think about how a human solves a problem with paper and pencil. First you **write the input on a paper**. Then you **do the computation** — you think, and you write intermediate results on the paper as you go. Finally you **write the output on the paper**. Everything you need is captured by three activities: reading/writing marks, moving your attention across the page, and changing what you are thinking about.

Turing abstracted exactly these activities into a machine. The name 'Turing' honors Alan Mathison Turing, and 'Machine' simply means a computing machine. The genius of the model is that these humble ingredients — marks on paper, a moving focus of attention, and a changing mental state — turn out to be powerful enough to capture *any* mechanical computation. In the segments that follow, we translate each human activity into a precise machine component.

practice.question: List the four qualities Turing wanted his model of computation to have, and name the three activities a human performs when computing on paper.
practice.hint: Look at Turing's stated aim and the 'How does a human compute?' steps.
practice.model_answer: The four qualities are: simple, intuitive, generic, and formalizes computation performed by a human mind. The three human activities are: writing the input on a paper, doing the computation (thinking and writing intermediate results), and writing the output on the paper.

segments.title: From human computation to machine parts
segments.content:
Building on the human analogy, Turing mapped each human activity onto a machine component. The **paper** becomes the **tape** — it simulates unlimited sheets of paper for computation. The **pencil/hand** becomes the **tape head**, which can read and write onto a single tape cell and move left or right. The **thinking mind** becomes the machine's **states**, which simulate the states of a human mind.

With these parts, the machine performs up to three operations at each step:
- **Write**: it optionally writes a new symbol at the current tape position.
- **Move**: it optionally moves the head either left or right.
- **Think**: it optionally changes to a new state.

The finite control (drawn as a box containing states like q0, q1, q2, q3, and h) directs these operations. The tape is drawn as a row of cells; the first cell holds a special left-end marker, followed by input symbols, and then blanks stretching to the right.

Summarizing the correspondence: the **input** is the finite set of symbols initially on the tape; the **output** is the finite set of symbols finally on the tape; and **computation** is a series of state transitions based on rules and the symbols read. This gives us the intuitive picture we will now make mathematically precise.

segments.title: The formal 6-tuple definition
segments.content:
We now state the TM precisely. A **Turing machine M is a 6-tuple** M = (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q0, H):

1. **Q**: a finite set of states.
2. **Σ**: the input alphabet, a finite set that *excludes* ▷, □, ←, and →.
3. **Γ**: the tape alphabet, a finite set with Σ ∪ {▷, □} ⊆ Γ, and Γ excludes ← and →.
4. **δ**: the transition function δ: (Q−H)×Γ → Q×(Γ∪{←,→}), constrained so the tape head never falls off the left end or erases the ▷ symbol. This function drives time (the computation).
5. **q0**: the start state, belonging to Q.
6. **H = {q_acc, q_rej}**: the set of halting states, a subset of Q.

Notice the domain of δ excludes halting states: δ is defined only on (Q−H). This means once the machine enters a halting state, no move is defined and it stops. Notice also that δ's output pairs a new state with *either* a symbol to write *or* a movement (←/→) — a single step either writes or moves, but the state can change either way. This compact definition captures everything from the previous segment's picture.

practice.question: In the transition function δ: (Q−H)×Γ → Q×(Γ∪{←,→}), why is the domain restricted to (Q−H) rather than all of Q, and what does the codomain tell you about a single step?
practice.hint: Recall what happens when the machine reaches a halting state, and what a step can produce.
practice.model_answer: The domain is restricted to (Q−H) because δ is not defined for halting states — when the machine reaches an accept or reject state it stops, so no transition should exist from them. The codomain Q×(Γ∪{←,→}) shows that each step moves to a new state and produces either a symbol to write (from Γ) or a movement (← or →), so a single step either writes a symbol or moves the head, while updating the state.

segments.title: Symbols and transition rules in practice
segments.content:
To read TMs fluently you must know the special symbols and rules. The symbols are: **▷** the left-end symbol; **□** the blank symbol; **←, →** the left and right movement symbols; **Σ** representing input/output/special symbols; and **Γ** representing all symbols that can appear on the tape.

Two transition rules follow from the definition. First, **M never falls off the left end of the tape**: whenever the current symbol is ▷, the head must move right. This keeps the machine on the tape. Second, **M stops when it reaches an accept or reject state**, because δ is not defined for states in H.

In worked examples the transition function is usually written as a table: rows are current states (from Q−H), columns are current symbols (from Γ), and each cell gives a (new-state, action) pair, where the action is either a symbol to write or a direction to move. A cell may be left blank or marked '−', meaning the machine terminates in the reject state q_rej for that combination. Equivalently, a state diagram draws a node per state and labels an edge from qi to qj with (read-symbol, action). Learning to switch between the table and the diagram is essential for the constructions that follow.

segments.title: Worked construction: erasing a string
segments.content:
Some tasks cannot be done by weaker machines. **DFAs are language recognizers** and **CFGs are language generators**; neither can perform a computational task like *erasing* a string. Because TMs are more powerful than both, a TM *can* erase strings.

Here is the erasing TM with states q0, q1, and halting state qh. The transition table is:
- q0: on ▷ → (q0, →); on a → (q1, □); on □ → (qh, □)
- q1: on a → (q0, a); on □ → (q0, →)

Read this as: q0 scans right past ▷, and when it sees an 'a' it erases it (writes □) and switches to q1; q1 then moves right (□→ means move right on blank) back to q0 to find the next symbol; when q0 finally reads a blank (meaning the input is fully erased) it halts.

Tracing input 'aaa' (tape ▷aaa□…): at time 0 q0 reads ▷ and moves right; it reads the first 'a' and erases it entering q1; the machine bounces between q0 and q1, erasing each 'a' in turn, until at time 8 it reaches qh with tape ▷□□□□…. The string has been erased. This demonstrates the write-move-think loop in action.

practice.question: Using the erasing TM's rule that q0 on symbol 'a' goes to (q1, □), explain in words what physically happens to the tape and state in that single step.
practice.hint: Recall that the second component of the output is either a symbol to write or a movement.
practice.model_answer: In that step the head is over a cell containing 'a'. The action □ means the machine writes a blank into that cell, erasing the 'a', and it changes its state from q0 to q1. The head does not move in this step; it only writes and changes state. State q1 then handles moving right to continue scanning.

segments.title: TM for a regular language: recognizing more than DFAs
segments.content:
TMs can also recognize any regular language, and they do so with an interesting twist. Consider L = {strings containing ab or ending with ba}, matching ((a|b)*ab(a|b)*)|((a|b)*ba). A DFA for this uses states q1–q5. The TM version starts at q0 (reading ▷, moving right into q1) and mimics the DFA transitions, but it moves the head right on each symbol and jumps to q_acc when acceptance is guaranteed.

The TM's transition table has states q0–q5. For example q1 on 'a'→(q2,→), on 'b'→(q4,→); q2 on 'a'→(q2,→), on 'b'→(q3,→); q3 accepts on any of a, b, □ by moving to q_acc; q4 on 'a'→(q5,→), on 'b'→(q4,→); q5 on 'a'→(q2,→), on 'b'→(q3,→), on □→(q_acc,→).

Tracing 'bba' the machine reaches q_acc; tracing 'bbb' it reaches q_rej (an undefined transition). A striking feature appears with 'aabbbbb': once the substring 'ab' is detected the TM enters q3 and moves to q_acc **without scanning the rest of the string**. Unlike a DFA or CFG, a TM can accept a string without reading it completely — it can stop as soon as the answer is determined.

segments.title: Varying TM features and computational power
segments.content:
What if we cripple a TM by removing some of its abilities? Consider machines defined by which of three features they have — left movement (←), right movement (→), and write. The full-power machine (← ✓, → ✓, write ✓) is a genuine Turing machine, the most powerful in this table.

The exercise poses several restricted variants: right-move-only without writing (✗←, ✓→, ✗write); both movements without writing (✓←, ✓→, ✗write); write only without any movement (✗←, ✗→, ✓write); and right movement with write but no left movement (✗←, ✓→, ✓write). Each raises the question: what computational power remains? The lesson is that a machine that can only move right and cannot write behaves like a read-once left-to-right scanner (essentially a finite automaton), while removing the ability to move backward or to rewrite the tape strictly reduces power. Only when a machine can move in **both** directions **and** write does it reach full Turing-machine power. This highlights that the *combination* of an unbounded tape, bidirectional movement, and writing is what gives the TM its strength.

practice.question: According to the feature table, which combination of the three features (left movement, right movement, write) yields a full Turing machine, and why is bidirectional movement plus writing important?
practice.hint: Only one row in the table is labeled 'TM'.
practice.model_answer: Only the machine with all three features — left movement (←) ✓, right movement (→) ✓, and write ✓ — is a full Turing machine. Bidirectional movement lets the head revisit and reprocess parts of the tape, and writing lets it record intermediate results and modify the tape. Without both, the machine cannot store and reuse information across the tape and its power drops to that of weaker models like finite automata.

segments.title: Worked construction: copying a string
segments.content:
Copying a string is another task beyond DFAs and CFGs but achievable by a TM. For L = Σ* with Σ = {a,b}, the copying TM uses tape alphabet Γ = Σ ∪ {▷, □, #, 1, 2}. The extra symbols are bookkeeping: '#' marks the boundary between the original and its copy; '1' and '2' temporarily mark an 'a' or 'b' that is currently being copied.

The idea: q1 scans right to the end of input and writes '#' (entering q2), then q2 returns left to ▷. From q3 the machine picks the next unmarked symbol — an 'a' is marked '1' (go to q4), a 'b' is marked '2' (go to q5) — walks right past the '#' to the first blank, writes the matching symbol (q6 writes 'a' or 'b'), then walks back left (q6→q7) restoring the marked symbol to its original 'a' or 'b', and repeats via q3. When q3 sees '#' with nothing left to copy it moves to q_acc.

Tracing 'bba' produces, after many steps, the tape ▷bba#bba□…: the original 'bba' is preserved and an exact copy appears after the '#'. Cells marked '−' in the table mean the machine terminates in q_rej. This construction shows how auxiliary tape symbols let a TM remember its place while shuttling back and forth.

segments.title: Recognizing a non-context-free language: aⁿbⁿcⁿ
segments.content:
The language L = {aⁿbⁿcⁿ | n ≥ 1} = {abc, aabbcc, aaabbbccc, …} cannot be accepted by any DFA or any CFG — both facts are proved using the pumping lemma. But a TM accepts it.

The strategy is to cross off one 'a', one 'b', and one 'c' per pass, using marker symbols x, y, z (so Γ = Σ ∪ {▷, □, x, y, z}). Starting in q1 the machine marks an 'a' as x (entering q2), scans right past a's and y's to find a 'b' which it marks y (entering q3), scans right past b's and z's to find a 'c' which it marks z (entering q4), then returns left (q4) skipping over marked and unmarked symbols back to the leftmost unmarked 'a' and repeats via q1. When q1 finds a 'y' instead of an 'a' (all a's consumed), it enters q5, which scans right over remaining y's and z's; if only y's and z's remain and it reaches a blank, it accepts.

Tracing 'aabbcc': the tape evolves ▷aabbcc□ → ▷xaybzc□ → ▷xxyyzz□ and finally q_acc. Each 'a', 'b', 'c' has been matched one-to-one, guaranteeing equal counts. This is a hallmark example of a TM outclassing weaker models.

practice.question: Explain how the aⁿbⁿcⁿ Turing machine guarantees that the numbers of a's, b's, and c's are equal, referring to the marker symbols x, y, and z.
practice.hint: Think about what happens in one full pass and what the machine checks at the end.
practice.model_answer: In each pass the machine marks exactly one 'a' as x, one 'b' as y, and one 'c' as z, thereby pairing them one-to-one. It repeats passes until no unmarked 'a' remains. Because every 'a' consumed requires a matching 'b' and 'c' to be marked in the same pass, the counts can only all reach zero simultaneously. At the end (state q5) it verifies that only y's and z's remain before the blank; if the numbers were unequal, some symbol would remain unmatched and the machine would fail to reach the accept state, ending in q_rej instead.

segments.title: Computation, configurations, and the yields relation
segments.content:
We can now name the pieces of a TM run precisely. A **configuration** captures all the information about the machine at one instant: the current state, the tape-head position, and the tape content — for example (q4, ▷bbb□). A run passes through configurations C0, C1, C2, … We distinguish the **starting** configuration, and **accepting/rejecting/halting** configurations.

A **computation** is a sequence of successive configurations linked by the **yields** relation ⊢M: C0 ⊢M C1 ⊢M C2 ⊢M … ⊢M Cn, where each ⊢M is one legal step of δ. The **computation time (or length)** is the number of steps; a five-step run is written C0 ⊢⁵M C5. The reflexive-transitive form ⊢*M means 'yields in zero or more steps', e.g., C1 ⊢*M C4.

This vocabulary reframes everything: running a TM is nothing but generating a sequence of configurations. That perspective is powerful. Indeed, one can speculate that a computer's operation is a sequence of computer states (a computation), that the human brain's ~86 billion neurons and their connections produce sequences of configurations (a giant computation), and that even the universe's atoms might follow a sequence of configurations (a gigantic computation). If such systems are computations, they can in principle be simulated on a real computer given enough memory and processing power. The biggest assumption underlying the TM definition is **finiteness**.

segments.title: Comparing DFAs, PDAs, and TMs
segments.content:
It helps to place the TM against the automata you already know. The document's comparison table lines them up feature by feature:

- **Memory size**: DFA finite; PDA infinite; TM infinite.
- **Halts?**: DFA always; PDA always; TM sometimes halts, sometimes not (✓,✗).
- **Input scanning**: DFA and PDA left-to-right; TM arbitrary.
- **Number of passes**: DFA and PDA one pass; TM any number.
- **Halting condition**: DFA/PDA at end of input; TM at an accept state.
- **Computing power**: DFA least; PDA medium; TM highest.
- **Language recognizer?**: all three yes.
- **Function calculator?**: only the TM (DFA and PDA cannot).
- **Decide RLs (regular languages)?**: all three yes.
- **Decide CFLs (context-free languages)?**: DFA no; PDA and TM yes.
- **Decide RELs (recursively enumerable languages)?**: only the TM.

The key takeaways: the TM's arbitrary, multi-pass scanning and its ability to halt at an accept state (rather than only at input's end) give it the highest computing power, the unique ability to compute functions, and the ability to decide the widest class of languages. Crucially, unlike the others, a TM may fail to halt.

practice.question: Give three ways, according to the comparison table, in which a TM is strictly more powerful or more flexible than a DFA.
practice.hint: Consider input scanning, passes, function computation, and the language classes each can decide.
practice.model_answer: Three ways: (1) A TM can scan its input arbitrarily and in any number of passes, whereas a DFA scans strictly left-to-right in a single pass. (2) A TM can act as a function calculator, while a DFA cannot (a DFA is only a language recognizer). (3) A TM can decide context-free languages and recursively enumerable languages, whereas a DFA can only decide regular languages. (A TM also has infinite memory versus a DFA's finite memory, but may not always halt.)

segments.title: Building complicated TMs from simpler ones
segments.content:
Just as large programs are built from smaller subroutines, complicated TMs are built from simpler TMs arranged using the **structure of a finite automaton**. In this construction the *nodes* of the automaton are themselves simpler TMs. A connection Mi —k→ Mj means: when TM Mi halts and the current tape symbol is k, then TM Mj starts.

For instance, a start machine M1 might branch: on tape symbol 'a' hand control to M2, and on tape symbol 'b' hand control to M3. Each of M1, M2, M3 is a full little TM doing part of the job, and the labeled arrows sequence them based on what symbol is under the head when a component halts.

This modular approach mirrors good software engineering: design and verify small, well-understood machines (e.g., 'move right to the next blank', 'copy a symbol', 'erase'), then wire them together. It makes complex behaviors — like the copying and aⁿbⁿcⁿ machines — easier to design and reason about. It also foreshadows the idea that TMs can be composed and, ultimately, that one TM can be built to run others.

segments.title: Universal Turing Machines and the compiler analogy
segments.content:
The composition idea culminates in the **Universal Turing Machine (UTM)**. A UTM MU can **simulate the execution of any TM M on any input w**. Given an encoding ⟨M, w⟩, the UTM U(⟨M,w⟩) **halts iff M halts on w**; if M is a deciding/semideciding machine then U accepts when M accepts and rejects when M rejects; and if M computes a function then U(⟨M,w⟩) equals M(w). A related theorem states that for any TM M and input w there exists a TM M′ that simulates M on w, halting iff M halts and returning the same result.

Thus a universal TM accepts L = {⟨M,w⟩ | M is a TM and w ∈ L(M)}. Strikingly, the analogous universal machines for weaker models **do not exist**: there is no universal DFA accepting {⟨M,w⟩ | M is a DFA and w ∈ L(M)} and no universal CFG for the CFG version — the answer to both is **No**, because those weaker models lack the power to simulate arbitrary members of their own class.

A concrete analogy: if you invent a new programming language X, can you write X's compiler *in X*? The answer is **Yes** — this 'self-hosting' or bootstrapping is precisely the universal-machine idea, where a system in a language is powerful enough to process programs of that same language. The UTM is the theoretical foundation of stored-program computers: one machine that can run any program.

practice.question: State what a Universal Turing Machine does and explain why a universal TM exists but a universal DFA does not.
practice.hint: Recall the working of U(⟨M,w⟩) and the comparison of computing power between TMs and DFAs.
practice.model_answer: A Universal Turing Machine MU takes an encoding ⟨M,w⟩ of any TM M and input w and simulates M on w: it halts iff M halts on w, accepts/rejects as M does, and returns M(w) if M computes a function. It accepts L = {⟨M,w⟩ | M is a TM and w ∈ L(M)}. A universal TM exists because a TM is powerful enough (infinite tape, arbitrary bidirectional scanning, writing) to store and simulate the description of any TM. A universal DFA does not exist because a DFA has only finite memory and one-pass left-to-right scanning, so it cannot store and simulate the transition behavior of an arbitrary DFA on arbitrary input — the class is too weak to contain a machine that simulates all its members.

rubric.concept: Formal definition of a Turing machine
key_points: A TM is a 6-tuple M = (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q0, H)
Q is the finite set of states; q0 ∈ Q is the start state; H = {q_acc, q_rej} is the set of halting states
Σ is the input alphabet excluding ▷, □, ←, →; Γ is the tape alphabet with Σ ∪ {▷,□} ⊆ Γ
δ: (Q−H)×Γ → Q×(Γ∪{←,→}) is the transition function; δ is undefined on halting states
Head never falls off the left end (must move right on ▷) and never erases ▷
Turing aimed for a model that is simple, intuitive, generic, and formalizes human mental computation
Paper → tape (unlimited storage); hand/pencil → tape head (read/write, moves left/right); mind → states
Each step involves Write, Move, and Think operations
Input is symbols initially on the tape; output is symbols finally on the tape
A configuration = current state + head position + tape content, e.g., (q4, ▷bbb□)
A computation is a sequence of configurations linked by the yields relation ⊢M; ⊢*M means zero or more steps
Transition tables/diagrams map (state, symbol) to (new state, write-symbol or move); '−' means terminate in q_rej
A TM halts upon reaching q_acc or q_rej, and can accept a string without scanning it completely
DFAs (recognizers) and CFGs (generators) cannot perform tasks like erasing/copying; TMs can
Auxiliary tape symbols (e.g., #, 1, 2, x, y, z) are used to mark positions while the head shuttles back and forth
{aⁿbⁿcⁿ | n≥1} is neither regular nor context-free (pumping lemma) but is accepted by a TM by crossing off one a, one b, one c per pass
Complicated TMs are built from simpler TMs wired with a finite-automaton structure, where Mi —k→ Mj passes control when Mi halts on symbol k
DFA has finite memory; PDA and TM have infinite memory
DFA/PDA scan left-to-right in one pass and halt at end of input; TM scans arbitrarily, any number of passes, halts at accept state
TM has the highest computing power and is the only one that can compute functions
TM can decide regular, context-free, and recursively enumerable languages; a TM may not always halt
A UTM simulates any TM M on any input w given the encoding ⟨M,w⟩
U(⟨M,w⟩) halts iff M halts on w; accepts/rejects as M does; returns M(w) if M computes a function
A universal TM accepts L = {⟨M,w⟩ | M is a TM and w ∈ L(M)}
No universal DFA or universal CFG exists because those models are too weak to simulate arbitrary members of their own class
